title: State Space Models and Filtering
markdown: ## What this covers A time series is a sequence of observations $y_0, y_1, \dots, y_T$ taken through time. This chapter develops **state space models**, the framework this course uses to describe such a sequence: the idea that the data are noisy measurements of a hidden process that itself evolves as a Markov chain. It builds the vocabulary (filtering, smoothing, prediction), works through a gallery of concrete models — tracking, trend estimation, stochastic volatility, dynamic regression, and the classical AR(2) model for sunspot cycles — and then derives the **Kalman filter**, the algorithm that solves the filtering problem in closed form when the model is linear and Gaussian. It assumes comfort with joint and conditional densities, Bayes' rule, the multivariate normal distribution, and ordinary least squares. Nothing about time series is assumed. ## State space models ### The joint structure: a hidden chain, noisy measurements A state space model says that the data $\{Y_t\}$ are noisy measurements of a hidden (or *latent*) process $\{X_t\}$, and that the hidden process is **Markov**: the conditional distribution of $X_t$ given the whole past $X_0, \dots, X_{t-1}$ depends only on $X_{t-1}$. Write $p_0(x_0)$ for the density of $X_0$ and $p_t(x_t \mid x_{t-1})$ for the transition density of $X_t$ given $X_{t-1} = x_{t-1}$ (if this does not depend on $t$, the chain is *time homogeneous*). The joint density of the whole hidden path is then the usual Markov-chain factorization $$p_0(x_0)\,p_1(x_1\mid x_0)\cdots p_T(x_T\mid x_{T-1}) = p_0(x_0)\prod_{t=1}^T p_t(x_t\mid x_{t-1}).$$ The second ingredient is the measurement mechanism: conditionally on the entire hidden path $X_0=x_0,\dots,X_T=x_T$, the observations $Y_0,\dots,Y_T$ are **independent**, and each $Y_t$ depends only on $X_t$ — not on $X_s$ for $s\neq t$, and not on any other $Y_s$. Write $f_t(y_t\mid x_t)$ for this conditional density. Then the conditional joint density of the data given the whole hidden path is $\prod_{t=0}^T f_t(y_t\mid x_t)$, and putting the two pieces together, the full joint density of $X_0,Y_0,\dots,X_T,Y_T$ is $$p_0(x_0)\prod_{t=1}^T p_t(x_t\mid x_{t-1})\;\prod_{t=0}^T f_t(y_t\mid x_t).$$ $X_0,\dots,X_T$ are the **state** (or hidden, or latent) variables; $Y_0,\dots,Y_T$ are the **data** variables. The density of the data alone is obtained, in principle, by integrating the display above over all the $x_t$'s — but doing this naively is exactly the computational problem this chapter is about. State space models are also called **Hidden Markov Models**, though some authors reserve that name for the case where the state is discrete. ### Two ways to specify a model In practice nobody writes down $p_0$, $p_t(\cdot\mid\cdot)$ and $f_t(\cdot\mid\cdot)$ directly. Instead one specifies $X_0$'s distribution, and then writes the evolution and the measurement as equations driven by independent noise: $$X_t = K_t(X_{t-1}, U_t) \quad (t = 1, 2, \dots), \qquad Y_t = H_t(X_t, V_t) \quad (t = 0, 1, \dots),$$ where $\{U_t\}$ are independent of each other and of $X_0$, and $\{V_t\}$ are independent of each other, of $\{U_t\}$, and of $X_0$. The functions $K_t$ and $H_t$ can be completely arbitrary — this is what makes state space models so widely applicable. The special case that makes inference tractable is the **linear Gaussian state space model**: $X_0$ is Gaussian, and $$X_t = A_t X_{t-1} + U_t, \qquad U_t \sim N(0,\Sigma_t), \qquad Y_t = B_t X_t + V_t, \qquad V_t \sim N(0,R_t),$$ with $X_0, U_1, \dots, V_0, V_1, \dots$ all independent, and $A_t, B_t$ deterministic matrices. Every one of $p_0$, $p_t(\cdot\mid\cdot)$, $f_t(\cdot\mid\cdot)$ is then Gaussian, with mean linear in the conditioning variable and covariance not depending on it. Most of this chapter builds toward the **Kalman filter**, the algorithm that exploits this structure. ## A gallery of state space models ### Tracking Suppose an object moves in the plane and we take noisy position measurements every $\delta$ time units. Let $(x_{1k},x_{2k})$ be its true position and $(x_{3k},x_{4k})$ its velocity at time $k\delta$. If velocity is nearly constant over $[(k-1)\delta,k\delta]$, $$x_{1k}\approx x_{1,k-1}+\delta x_{3,k-1}, \qquad x_{2k}\approx x_{2,k-1}+\delta x_{4,k-1},$$ and similarly $x_{3k}\approx x_{3,k-1}$, $x_{4k}\approx x_{4,k-1}$ if acceleration is small. Turning the approximations into exact equations by adding noise terms $q_{1k},\dots,q_{4k}\stackrel{\text{i.i.d}}{\sim}N(0,\cdot)$ and stacking $X_k = (x_{1k},x_{2k},x_{3k},x_{4k})'$ gives $$X_k = \begin{pmatrix} 1&0&\delta&0\\0&1&0&\delta\\0&0&1&0\\0&0&0&1 \end{pmatrix} X_{k-1} + q_k,$$ a Markov chain. If we measure only position, $Y_k = \begin{pmatrix}1&0&0&0\\0&1&0&0\end{pmatrix}X_k+\epsilon_k$ with $\epsilon_k\stackrel{\text{i.i.d}}{\sim}N(0,\cdot)$ independent of $\{q_k\}$: a **linear Gaussian** state space model. If instead only the bearing to the object is measured (*bearings-only tracking*), $$Y_k = \arctan\!\left(\frac{x_{2k}}{x_{1k}}\right) + \epsilon_k,$$ which is a state space model but a **nonlinear** one — the Kalman filter of later sections does not apply directly to it. ### Trend estimation: the local level model State space models can also extract a smooth trend from a noisy series. Let the hidden states $X_0,\dots,X_T$ represent the trend, forced to move smoothly by a random walk, $$X_t = X_{t-1}+\eta_t, \qquad \eta_t\stackrel{\text{i.i.d}}{\sim}N(0,\sigma_\eta^2),$$ and let the data track the trend with observation noise, $$Y_t = X_t + \epsilon_t, \qquad \epsilon_t\stackrel{\text{i.i.d}}{\sim}N(0,\sigma_\epsilon^2).$$ This pair of equations is the **local level model**. Small $\sigma_\eta$ forces $X_t\approx X_{t-1}$ (a smooth trend); small $\sigma_\epsilon$ forces the trend to hug the data closely. The two cannot both be made small if the data are genuinely rough, so in practice $\sigma_\eta,\sigma_\epsilon$ are chosen to fit the data well — the subject of a later section. ### A smoother trend: the local linear model The local level trend is often visibly wiggly. A smoother alternative puts the random walk on the *slope* rather than the level: $$X_t - X_{t-1} = (X_{t-1}-X_{t-2}) + \eta_t, \qquad \eta_t\stackrel{\text{i.i.d}}{\sim}N(0,\sigma_\eta^2), \qquad Y_t = X_t+\epsilon_t.$$ As written, $\{X_t\}$ alone is not Markov — the increment depends on two past values. But it becomes one after augmenting the state to $\tilde X_t := (X_t, X_{t-1})'$, since the slope equation is equivalent to $$\tilde X_t = \begin{pmatrix}2&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}\tilde X_{t-1} + \begin{pmatrix}\eta_t\\0\end{pmatrix}, \qquad Y_t = \begin{pmatrix}1&0\end{pmatrix}\tilde X_t + \epsilon_t.$$ This trick — augmenting the state to turn a higher-order recursion into a first-order Markov one — is the discrete-time analogue of rewriting a second-order ODE $x''(t)=-\omega^2 x(t)$ as the first-order system $\begin{pmatrix}x_1'\\x_2'\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-\omega^2&0\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}x_1\\x_2\end{pmatrix}$. The same device reappears throughout this chapter. ### Stochastic volatility $$X_t = X_{t-1}+\eta_t, \qquad \eta_t\stackrel{\text{i.i.d}}{\sim}N(0,\sigma_\eta^2), \qquad Y_t = e^{X_t/2}\epsilon_t, \qquad \epsilon_t\stackrel{\text{i.i.d}}{\sim}N(0,\sigma_\epsilon^2).$$ Here the hidden state controls the *scale* of the observation rather than its location, so realizations show **volatility clustering** — the variance stays high or low for stretches of time — which makes this a natural model for financial log-returns. It is a state space model, but not a linear Gaussian one (the observation equation is multiplicative), and it is a more natural alternative to the ARCH and GARCH family of volatility models. ### Dynamic (time-varying) regression For a response $y_t$ and a deterministic covariate $x_t$, allow the regression coefficients themselves to drift: $$y_t = \alpha_t+\beta_t x_t+\epsilon_t, \qquad \alpha_t=\alpha_{t-1}+w_{\alpha,t}, \qquad \beta_t=\beta_{t-1}+w_{\beta,t},$$ with the noises independent and Gaussian. Writing $S_t=(\alpha_t,\beta_t)'$, this is a state space model with $S_t = S_{t-1}+(w_{\alpha t},w_{\beta t})'$ and $Y_t = (1\;\; x_t)S_t+\epsilon_t$. One use: $y_t$ the return on a stock, $x_t$ the return on the market, so the fitted $\beta_t$ tracks how the stock's market exposure evolves over time. ## Case study: is there really an eleven-year sunspot cycle? Historically the AR(2) model (developed below) was introduced by Yule (1927) for the sunspot number series, which is often said to follow an approximately 11-year cycle. Before building the autoregressive model, it is worth working through a direct Bayesian treatment of the simplest periodic model, because it both illustrates a genuinely useful trick — integrating out nuisance parameters analytically — and connects to a standard object in time series, the periodogram. Fit a single sinusoid plus noise to sunspot counts $(t_1,y_1),\dots,(t_n,y_n)$: $$Y_i = \mu+\alpha_1\cos(\omega t_i)+\alpha_2\sin(\omega t_i)+\epsilon_i, \qquad \epsilon_i\stackrel{\text{i.i.d}}{\sim}N(0,\sigma^2).$$ The parameter of interest is the frequency $\omega$ (an 11-year cycle predicts $\omega\approx 2\pi/11\approx0.5712$); $\mu,\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\sigma$ are nuisance parameters. Take independent diffuse priors, $$\omega,\mu,\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\log\sigma \stackrel{\text{i.i.d}}{\sim}\mathrm{Unif}(-C,C)$$ for large $C$ (a uniform prior on $\log\sigma$ is the standard diffuse choice for a scale parameter; by the change-of-variables formula it corresponds to the density $f_\sigma(x)\propto 1/x$ on $\sigma\in(e^{-C},e^C)$). Writing $Y=(y_1,\dots,y_n)'$, $\beta=(\mu,\alpha_1,\alpha_2)'$, and $X(\omega)$ for the $n\times 3$ design matrix with rows $(1,\cos(\omega t_i),\sin(\omega t_i))$, the model is $Y=X(\omega)\beta+\epsilon$, and the posterior, up to the constant $C$, is $$f_{\omega,\beta,\sigma\mid\text{data}}(\omega,\beta,\sigma) \propto \sigma^{-n-1}\exp\!\left(-\frac{\|Y-X(\omega)\beta\|^2}{2\sigma^2}\right).$$ To get the marginal posterior for $\omega$, integrate out $\beta$ and $\sigma$. Let $\hat\beta(\omega) = (X'X)^{-1}X'Y$ be the least squares estimator for fixed $\omega$; then $\|Y-X\beta\|^2 = \|Y-X\hat\beta\|^2+(\beta-\hat\beta)'X'X(\beta-\hat\beta)$. The $\beta$-integral is a multivariate normal normalizing constant, $$\int_{\mathbb{R}^3}\exp\!\left(-\frac{(\beta-\hat\beta)'X'X(\beta-\hat\beta)}{2\sigma^2}\right)d\beta = (2\pi)^{3/2}\sigma^3(\det X'X)^{-1/2},$$ leaving $\int_0^\infty \sigma^{-n+2}\exp(-\|Y-X\hat\beta\|^2/2\sigma^2)\,d\sigma \propto \|Y-X\hat\beta\|^{-(n-3)}$ after the substitution $t=\sigma/\|Y-X\hat\beta\|$ (this integral contributes only a constant, since it does not depend on $\omega$ once the residual norm is factored out). Altogether, $$f_{\omega\mid\text{data}}(\omega) \propto (\det X(\omega)'X(\omega))^{-1/2}\,\|Y-X(\omega)\hat\beta(\omega)\|^{-(n-3)},$$ a function of $\omega$ computable on a grid. ### Connection to the periodogram The **periodogram** of the data is $$I(\omega) := \frac1n\left[\left(\sum_j y_j\cos(\omega t_j)\right)^2+\left(\sum_j y_j\sin(\omega t_j)\right)^2\right] = \frac1n\left|\sum_j y_j e^{i\omega t_j}\right|^2,$$ the squared modulus (scaled by $n$) of the **discrete Fourier transform** $b(\omega):=\sum_j y_je^{i\omega t_j}$. For equally spaced data $t_j=j-1$, the periodogram is usually only evaluated at the **Fourier frequencies** $\omega=2\pi k/n$, $k=1,\dots,n-1$. The posterior above is secretly a function of the periodogram. The matrix $X(\omega)'X(\omega)$ has entries built from $\sum\cos$, $\sum\sin$, $\sum\cos^2$, $\sum\sin^2$, $\sum\cos\sin$; at (or near) a Fourier frequency these are well approximated by $\mathrm{diag}(n,\,n/2,\,n/2)$. For instance, $$\frac1n\sum_{j=1}^n\cos^2(\omega t_j) = \frac12+\frac1{4n}\sum_j e^{2i\omega t_j}+\frac1{4n}\sum_j e^{-2i\omega t_j},$$ and each geometric sum $\sum_j e^{\pm2i\omega(j-1)} = \frac{e^{\pm2i\omega n}-1}{e^{\pm2i\omega}-1}$ vanishes exactly when $\omega=2\pi k/n$ (since then $e^{\pm2i\omega n}=1$), and is small whenever $n|e^{\pm2i\omega}-1|$ is large — i.e. for a generic $\omega$ not too close to $0$. The other four entries of $X'X$ vanish or converge to $n/2$ by the same kind of computation. Once $X'X\approx\mathrm{diag}(n,n/2,n/2)$, the quadratic form $\|Y-X\beta\|^2$ decouples into three independent one-dimensional pieces in $\mu,\alpha_1,\alpha_2$, and the $\beta$-integral factors into three separate Gaussian integrals of the form $\int\exp(xC_1-\tfrac{C_2}2x^2)\,dx=\sqrt{2\pi/C_2}\exp(C_1^2/2C_2)$. Carrying this out and collecting terms, the exponent that survives is $$-\frac1{2\sigma^2}\sum_i y_i^2+\frac{(\sum_iy_i)^2}{2n\sigma^2}+\frac{(\sum_iy_i\cos\omega t_i)^2+(\sum_iy_i\sin\omega t_i)^2}{n\sigma^2} = -\frac1{\sigma^2}\left[\frac{\sum_i(y_i-\bar y)^2}{2}-I(\omega)\right],$$ using $\sum y_i^2-(\sum y_i)^2/n=\sum(y_i-\bar y)^2$ and the definition of $I(\omega)$. Integrating out $\sigma$ exactly as before gives, with $S:=\sum_i(y_i-\bar y)^2$, $$f_{\omega\mid\text{data}}(\omega) \propto \left[\frac{S}{2}-I(\omega)\right]^{-(n-3)/2} \propto \left[1-\frac{2I(\omega)}{S}\right]^{-(n-3)/2}.$$ So the Bayesian posterior for $\omega$ is a specific, sharply peaked transform of the periodogram — not the periodogram itself. For the sunspots series the raw periodogram has several peaks, but this posterior concentrates strongly, which is exactly the behaviour wanted when the question is "what is *the* dominant frequency" rather than "which frequencies are present at all." ## From a single sinusoid to autoregression The single-sinusoid model fits the sunspot series poorly: the residual amplitude is too irregular for one clean cycle, and simulated data from it look noisier than the real series does. Yule's 1927 alternative starts from a different way of characterizing a sinusoid. ### A sinusoid as the solution of a difference equation Let $s_t=\mu+\alpha_1\cos(\omega t)+\alpha_2\sin(\omega t)$. In continuous time, $s(t)$ solves $s''(t)=-\omega^2(s(t)-\mu)$. The discrete analogue, obtained from the trig identity $\cos(A+B)-2\cos A+\cos(A-B) = 2\cos A(\cos B-1)$ applied with $A=\omega(t+1)$, $B=\omega$ (and the matching identity for $\sin$), is $$s_{t+2}-2s_{t+1}+s_t = 2(\cos\omega-1)(s_{t+1}-\mu).$$ Conversely, every solution of this recursion with given $s_0,s_1$ is of the sinusoidal form above for some $\alpha_1,\alpha_2$: matching a trial sinusoid $h_t=\alpha_1\cos(\omega t)+\alpha_2\sin(\omega t)$ to $g_t:=s_t-\mu$ at $t=0,1$ forces $h_t$ to satisfy the same two-term recursion as $g_t$ (using the double-angle identities), so $h_t=g_t$ for every subsequent $t$ by induction. Rearranged, the recursion reads $s_{t+2}=(2\cos\omega)s_{t+1}-s_t+2(1-\cos\omega)\mu$. Yule proposed building a noisy model directly from this equation, $$Y_{t+2} = \theta Y_{t+1}-Y_t+c+Z_{t+2}, \qquad Z_{t+2}\stackrel{\text{i.i.d}}{\sim}N(0,\sigma^2). \tag{Yule}$$ ### Two places noise can enter To see why this is a genuinely different model from the earlier sinusoid-plus-noise one, consider the physical source of a sinusoid: a mass on a spring on a frictionless surface. Hooke's law and Newton's second law give $-\kappa y(t)=my''(t)$, i.e. $y''(t)=-\omega^2y(t)$ with $\omega=\sqrt{\kappa/m}$, whose solutions are exactly the sinusoids $\alpha_1\cos(\omega t)+\alpha_2\sin(\omega t)$. Suppose we measure the displacement $y(t)$ at a sequence of times. - **Measurement noise** (the earlier model, $Y_t=\mu+\alpha_1\cos(\omega t)+\alpha_2\sin(\omega t)+\epsilon_t$): the oscillation is perfectly sinusoidal, but every reading is corrupted by an independent error. - **Process noise** (Yule's model above): the measurement is exact, but the oscillation itself is not perfectly sinusoidal — as Yule put it, imagine children randomly throwing stones at the mass, from the left or the right, while it swings. Data generated from the process-noise model are visibly smoother than data generated from the measurement-noise model, because a single noisy perturbation to the trajectory keeps propagating through the deterministic part of the recursion, rather than being independently redrawn at every time point. Yule used this observation to argue that his model is the better description of the sunspot series. It is natural to want both kinds of error at once, and this again produces a state space model — with hidden $X_t=\theta X_{t-1}-X_{t-2}+c+Z_t$ evolving smoothly and $Y_t=X_t+\epsilon_t$ adding measurement error on top, Markov once the state is augmented to $(X_t,X_{t-1})'$ as in the local linear model above. ### The AR(2) model and damped sinusoids Yule went further and fit a model more general than (Yule): the **autoregressive model of order 2**, $$Y_{t+2} = \phi_1Y_{t+1}+\phi_2Y_t+c+Z_{t+2},$$ of which (Yule) is the special case $\phi_2=-1$. Fit to the sunspots series for 1700–1969, this gives (numerically) $Y_{t+2}=23.92+1.38\,Y_{t+1}-0.69\,Y_t+Z_{t+2}$, so future values are forecast by recursing $Y_t=23.92+1.38\,Y_{t-1}-0.69\,Y_{t-2}$. Centering at the fitted mean $77.16$ (note $77.16(1-1.38+0.69)\approx 23.92$) turns this into a homogeneous recursion for $U_t:=Y_t-77.16$, $$U_t = 1.38\,U_{t-1}-0.69\,U_{t-2}.$$ **Fact.** *For the recursion $U_t=\phi_1U_{t-1}+\phi_2U_{t-2}$ with given initial values, if the polynomial $1-\phi_1z-\phi_2z^2$ has complex conjugate roots $z_1,z_2=re^{\pm i\theta}$, then the solution has the form* $$U_t = c_1\,r^{-t}\cos(\theta t+c_2)$$ *for constants $c_1,c_2$ fixed by the initial conditions.* *Why.* Write $H_t=c_1r^{-t}\cos(\theta t+c_2)$; using Euler's formula this is $H_t = c_1e^{ic_2}z_1^{-t}+c_1e^{-ic_2}z_2^{-t}$ (up to relabelling the constant). Substituting into the recursion, $$H_t-\phi_1H_{t-1}-\phi_2H_{t-2} = c_1e^{ic_2}z_1^{-t}(1-\phi_1z_1-\phi_2z_1^2)+c_1e^{-ic_2}z_2^{-t}(1-\phi_1z_2-\phi_2z_2^2)=0,$$ because $z_1,z_2$ are exactly the roots of $1-\phi_1z-\phi_2z^2$. So $H_t$ solves the same recursion; choosing $c_1,c_2$ to match $U_t$ at the two initial times makes $H_t=U_t$ for all later $t$ as well, since a second-order linear recursion is determined by two initial values. $\blacksquare$ For the fitted sunspots model, $1-1.38z+0.69z^2$ has complex roots giving $r\approx1.2$, $\theta\approx0.59$, so forecasts follow $c_1(1.2)^{-t}\cos(0.59t+c_2)$: a **damped sinusoid**, decaying toward the mean level rather than oscillating forever — a picture very different from, and generally more realistic than, a pure undamped sine wave. ## Filtering, smoothing, and prediction: the general picture Return to a general state space model, now written with an explicit unknown parameter $\theta$ (for the local level model, $\theta=(\sigma_\eta^2,\sigma_\epsilon^2)$), and take the fully Bayesian view: $\theta$ has a (typically diffuse) prior $f_\theta$, and "fitting the model" means finding the joint conditional distribution of everything unknown — $X_0,\dots,X_T$ and $\theta$ — given the data: $$f_{X_{0:T},\theta\mid\text{data}}(x_{0:T},\theta) \;\propto\; p_0(x_0\mid\theta)\prod_{t=1}^Tp_t(x_t\mid x_{t-1},\theta)\prod_{t=0}^Tf_t(y_t\mid x_t,\theta)\,f_\theta(\theta).$$ This high-dimensional density answers any question about $X_{0:T},\theta$ in principle, but what is usually wanted in practice is much smaller: the marginal conditional distribution of each individual state, $$X_t \mid Y_0=y_0,\dots,Y_T=y_T \qquad (t=0,\dots,T).$$ Naively marginalizing the full joint posterior to get this is computationally infeasible. The resolution is to split the problem in two, using $$f_{X_t\mid\text{data}}(x_t) = \int f_{X_t\mid\text{data},\theta}(x_t)\,f_{\theta\mid\text{data}}(\theta)\,d\theta,$$ i.e. (i) compute $X_t\mid\text{data},\theta$ for each fixed $\theta$, and (ii) compute $\theta\mid\text{data}$, which by Bayes' rule reduces to the **likelihood** $f_{Y_{0:T}\mid\theta}$. The conditional distributions $X_t\mid Y_0=y_0,\dots,Y_T=y_T,\theta$, for a fixed $\theta$, are called **smoothing distributions**. The rest of this chapter is about computing them (and the likelihood) efficiently. Three names are used depending on how the conditioning time $t$ compares to the state index $s$ of interest, $X_s\mid Y_0=y_0,\dots,Y_t=y_t,\theta$: - **filtering** ($s=t$): the current state given data up to now; - **smoothing** ($s\le t$): a past state given data collected after it too; - **prediction** ($s>t$): a future state given only data up to now. Tracking problems mostly care about filtering and prediction; trend estimation mostly cares about smoothing and prediction. The strategy for computing all the smoothing distributions is **forward filtering, backward smoothing (FFBS)**: first compute the filtering distributions $X_t\mid Y_0=y_0,\dots,Y_t=y_t,\theta$ recursively forward, for $t=0,1,\dots,T$; this immediately gives the *last* smoothing distribution ($s=T$) for free, since filtering and smoothing coincide at $s=t=T$. The remaining smoothing distributions are then obtained by a **backward** recursion from $s=T-1$ down to $s=0$. This chapter develops the forward (filtering) half in full, and for linear Gaussian models this specializes to the Kalman filter; the backward (smoothing) half is genuinely the next topic and is only outlined here — see the note at the end of the chapter. A model is called **linear Gaussian** if $p_0(\cdot\mid\theta)$ is Gaussian, $p_t(\cdot\mid x_{t-1},\theta)$ is Gaussian with mean linear in $x_{t-1}$ and covariance not depending on $x_{t-1}$, and likewise $f_t(\cdot\mid x_t,\theta)$ is Gaussian, linear in $x_t$, with covariance not depending on $x_t$ — the same condition given in matrix form earlier. For such models every filtering, smoothing and prediction distribution turns out to be Gaussian, so each is fully described by a mean and a covariance, and the general recursions below become recursions on those means and covariances. That specialization is the Kalman filter. ## The general filtering recursion Fix $\theta$ and drop it from the notation for readability. The recursive step goes from the filtering density at $t-1$, $f_{X_{t-1}\mid Y_{0:t-1}=y_{0:t-1}}(x_{t-1})$, to the filtering density at $t$, in two stages. **One-step prediction.** By the Markov property, $X_t$ given $X_{t-1}=x_{t-1}$ and the past data $Y_{0:t-1}=y_{0:t-1}$ has the same conditional density as $X_t$ given $X_{t-1}=x_{t-1}$ alone, namely $p_t(x_t\mid x_{t-1})$. Averaging over $x_{t-1}$ against its own filtering density gives the one-step predictive density: $$f_{X_t\mid Y_{0:t-1}=y_{0:t-1}}(x_t) = \int p_t(x_t\mid x_{t-1})\,f_{X_{t-1}\mid Y_{0:t-1}=y_{0:t-1}}(x_{t-1})\,dx_{t-1}.$$ **Filtering update.** By Bayes' rule, $$f_{X_t\mid Y_{0:t}=y_{0:t}}(x_t) \propto f_{Y_t\mid X_t=x_t,Y_{0:t-1}=y_{0:t-1}}(y_t)\,f_{X_t\mid Y_{0:t-1}=y_{0:t-1}}(x_t),$$ and, since $Y_t$ is conditionally independent of everything else given $X_t$, the first factor is just $f_t(y_t\mid x_t)$. So $$f_{X_t\mid Y_{0:t}=y_{0:t}}(x_t) = \frac{f_t(y_t\mid x_t)\,f_{X_t\mid Y_{0:t-1}=y_{0:t-1}}(x_t)}{\int f_t(y_t\mid u)\,f_{X_t\mid Y_{0:t-1}=y_{0:t-1}}(u)\,du}.$$ The recursion is initialized by applying the filtering update once with $f_{X_0}=p_0$ in place of the predictive density. Both steps are, in general, intractable integrals — but for the linear Gaussian model both can be solved in closed form, giving the Kalman filter. ## The Kalman filter Consider the linear Gaussian state space model $$X_0\sim N(\mu_0,\Gamma_0), \qquad X_t=A_tX_{t-1}+U_t,\;\;U_t\sim N(0,\Sigma_t), \qquad Y_t=B_tX_t+V_t,\;\;V_t\sim N(0,R_t),$$ with everything independent as before. Write $X_s\mid Y_{0:t}=y_{0:t}\sim N(m_{s\mid t},Q_{s\mid t})$ for the (Gaussian) conditional distributions of interest. The Kalman filter computes $m_{t\mid t}, Q_{t\mid t}$ recursively by solving the two steps above in closed form. ### Time update (predict) Conditionally on $Y_{0:t-1}=y_{0:t-1}$, $X_{t-1}\sim N(m_{t-1\mid t-1},Q_{t-1\mid t-1})$ and $U_t\sim N(0,\Sigma_t)$ independently, so $X_t=A_tX_{t-1}+U_t$ given the past data is a linear combination of independent Gaussians: $$m_{t\mid t-1}=A_tm_{t-1\mid t-1}, \qquad Q_{t\mid t-1}=A_tQ_{t-1\mid t-1}A_t'+\Sigma_t.$$ ### Measurement update (filter) The measurement update is an instance of the following general fact about Bayesian linear models. **Fact.** *If $X\sim N(m_0,Q_0)$ and $Y\mid X=x\sim N(Bx,R)$, then* $$X\mid Y=y \sim N(m_1,Q_1), \qquad m_1=(Q_0^{-1}+B'R^{-1}B)^{-1}(Q_0^{-1}m_0+B'R^{-1}y), \qquad Q_1=(Q_0^{-1}+B'R^{-1}B)^{-1}.$$ This is the familiar precision-weighted conjugate normal update, and two special cases confirm it is the right formula. With $m_0=\mu,Q_0=\tau^2$, $Y=(Y_1,\dots,Y_n)'$, $B=(1,\dots,1)'$, $R=\sigma^2I$, it reduces to the textbook posterior for a normal mean, $\Theta\mid Y\sim N\!\left(\frac{\mu/\tau^2+n\bar y/\sigma^2}{1/\tau^2+n/\sigma^2},\;\frac1{1/\tau^2+n/\sigma^2}\right)$. With $X=\beta\sim N(m_0,Q_0)$ and $Y\mid\beta\sim N(Z\beta,\sigma^2I)$ it gives the Bayesian linear regression posterior, which in the diffuse-prior limit $Q_0=CI,\,C\to\infty$ reduces to the ordinary least squares result $\beta\mid Y\approx N((Z'Z)^{-1}Z'Y,\,\sigma^2(Z'Z)^{-1})$, as it must. An algebraically equivalent form, obtained from the Sherman–Morrison–Woodbury identity $(A+UCV)^{-1}=A^{-1}-A^{-1}U(C^{-1}+VA^{-1}U)^{-1}VA^{-1}$, is $$m_1 = m_0+Q_0B'(BQ_0B'+R)^{-1}(y-Bm_0), \qquad Q_1 = Q_0-Q_0B'(BQ_0B'+R)^{-1}BQ_0.$$ The first form inverts a matrix the size of $X$; the second inverts a matrix the size of $Y$. When $Y$ has much lower dimension than $X$ — the usual case in tracking, where many state coordinates are inferred from one or two measured ones — the second form is far cheaper, and is the one used below. Applying the Fact with $m_0=m_{t\mid t-1}$, $Q_0=Q_{t\mid t-1}$, $B=B_t$, $R=R_t$ gives the Kalman filter's measurement update: $$m_{t\mid t} = m_{t\mid t-1}+Q_{t\mid t-1}B_t'(B_tQ_{t\mid t-1}B_t'+R_t)^{-1}(y_t-B_tm_{t\mid t-1}),$$ $$Q_{t\mid t} = Q_{t\mid t-1}-Q_{t\mid t-1}B_t'(B_tQ_{t\mid t-1}B_t'+R_t)^{-1}B_tQ_{t\mid t-1}.$$ ### The algorithm Given $\mu_0,\Gamma_0$ and $\{A_t\},\{B_t\},\{\Sigma_t\},\{R_t\}$: 1. **Initialize.** Set $m_{0\mid-1}=\mu_0$, $Q_{0\mid-1}=\Gamma_0$, and apply the measurement update once to get $m_{0\mid0},Q_{0\mid0}$. 2. **Recurse.** For $t=1,2,\dots$, apply the time update and then the measurement update. The recursion also produces the one-step-ahead predictive means and covariances $m_{t\mid t-1},Q_{t\mid t-1}$ as a byproduct — these are exactly the prediction distributions for $s=t+1$ relative to data through $t-1$, and, as the next sections show, they are also exactly what is needed to evaluate the likelihood. ## Worked examples of the Kalman filter ### Tracking with a velocity model An object moves on a line; its true position $x_k$ at time $k\Delta t$ is measured with noise, $y_k=x_k+\epsilon_k$, $\epsilon_k\stackrel{\text{i.i.d}}{\sim}N(0,\sigma_\epsilon^2)$. If velocity is constant at level $u_k\stackrel{\text{i.i.d}}{\sim}N(0,\sigma_u^2)$ over each interval, $x_k=x_{k-1}+u_k\Delta t$ — the local level model again, with state-noise variance $\sigma_u^2(\Delta t)^2$. With diffuse initialization $x_0\sim N(0,C)$, the Kalman recursion is $$m_{k\mid k-1}=m_{k-1\mid k-1}, \qquad Q_{k\mid k-1}=Q_{k-1\mid k-1}+\sigma_u^2(\Delta t)^2,$$ $$m_{k\mid k} = m_{k\mid k-1}+\frac{Q_{k\mid k-1}}{Q_{k\mid k-1}+\sigma_\epsilon^2}(y_k-m_{k\mid k-1}), \qquad Q_{k\mid k} = \frac{Q_{k\mid k-1}\sigma_\epsilon^2}{Q_{k\mid k-1}+\sigma_\epsilon^2}.$$ Starting from $m_{0\mid-1}=0,Q_{0\mid-1}=C$ gives $m_{0\mid0}=\frac{C}{C+\sigma_\epsilon^2}y_0\to y_0$ and $Q_{0\mid0}=\frac{C\sigma_\epsilon^2}{C+\sigma_\epsilon^2}\to\sigma_\epsilon^2$ as $C\to\infty$: the standard diffuse initialization for the local level model is simply $m_{0\mid0}=y_0,\,Q_{0\mid0}=\sigma_\epsilon^2$. ### Tracking with an acceleration model Now let acceleration $a_k\stackrel{\text{i.i.d}}{\sim}N(0,\sigma_a^2)$ be constant over each interval, with state $x_k=(x_{k,1},x_{k,2})'$ (position, velocity): $$x_{k,2}=x_{k-1,2}+a_k\Delta t, \qquad x_{k,1}=x_{k-1,1}+x_{k-1,2}\Delta t+\tfrac12(\Delta t)^2a_k,$$ which combine into $$x_k=\begin{pmatrix}1&\Delta t\\0&1\end{pmatrix}x_{k-1}+U_k, \qquad U_k\sim N\!\left(0,\;\sigma_a^2\begin{pmatrix}(\Delta t)^4/4&(\Delta t)^3/2\\(\Delta t)^3/2&(\Delta t)^2\end{pmatrix}\right), \qquad y_k=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\end{pmatrix}x_k+\epsilon_k.$$ The time update carries $m_{t\mid t-1},Q_{t\mid t-1}$ through the matrix $\begin{pmatrix}1&\Delta t\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ and adds the noise covariance above; the measurement update, writing $Q[i,j]$ for entries of $Q_{t\mid t-1}$, simplifies (since $B_t=(1\;\;0)$) to $$m_{t\mid t} = m_{t\mid t-1}+\frac{y_t-m_{t\mid t-1}[1]}{Q[1,1]+\sigma_\epsilon^2}\begin{pmatrix}Q[1,1]\\Q[2,1]\end{pmatrix}, \qquad Q_{t\mid t} = Q_{t\mid t-1}-\frac1{Q[1,1]+\sigma_\epsilon^2}\begin{pmatrix}Q[1,1]^2&Q[1,1]Q[2,1]\\Q[1,1]Q[2,2]&Q[2,1]^2\end{pmatrix}.$$ The general Kalman filter formulas cost nothing more than one matrix-vector multiply and one scalar division here, because there is only one observed coordinate. ### The local linear model recovered The local linear model of the gallery above can be seen as an approximation to the acceleration model when $\Delta t$ is small: drop the $\tfrac12(\Delta t)^2a_k$ term from the position equation (negligible next to the other two terms), leaving $x_{k,1}=x_{k-1,1}+x_{k-1,2}\Delta t$ and $x_{k,2}=x_{k-1,2}+a_k\Delta t$. Solving the first equation for velocity at consecutive times and substituting into the second gives $$x_{k+1,1}-2x_{k,1}+x_{k-1,1} = a_k(\Delta t)^2 \sim N(0,\sigma_a^2(\Delta t)^4),$$ exactly the local linear model's second-difference recursion, with state-noise variance $\sigma_a^2(\Delta t)^4$. It can be written in state space form either with $(x_{k,1},x_{k-1,1})$ as the state, or with $(x_{k,1},\,(\Delta t)^{-1}(x_{k,1}-x_{k-1,1}))$ (position and an estimated velocity) — a reminder that the same model can be put in state space form in more than one way (see the exercises). ## Using the Kalman filter for likelihood-based inference The unknown quantities in $\mu_0,\Gamma_0,A_t,B_t,\Sigma_t,R_t$ typically depend on a parameter vector $\theta$ that must be estimated from the data. The Kalman filter's output is exactly what is needed to write down the likelihood. By the chain rule for densities, $$f_{Y_{0:T}\mid\theta}(y_{0:T}) = \prod_{t=0}^T f_{Y_t\mid Y_{0:t-1}=y_{0:t-1},\theta}(y_t),$$ and, conditionally on the past data, $Y_t=B_tX_t+V_t$ is a sum of the independent Gaussians $X_t\sim N(m_{t\mid t-1},Q_{t\mid t-1})$ and $V_t\sim N(0,R_t)$, so $$Y_t\mid Y_{0:t-1}=y_{0:t-1},\theta \;\sim\; N\big(B_tm_{t\mid t-1},\;B_tQ_{t\mid t-1}B_t'+R_t\big).$$ Writing $\epsilon_t(\theta):=y_t-B_tm_{t\mid t-1}$ and $H_t(\theta):=B_tQ_{t\mid t-1}B_t'+R_t$ for the one-step-ahead prediction error and its variance, $$-2\log f_{Y_{0:T}\mid\theta}(y_{0:T}) = \sum_{t=0}^T\Big[\log|2\pi H_t(\theta)|+\epsilon_t(\theta)'H_t(\theta)^{-1}\epsilon_t(\theta)\Big].$$ Since $m_{t\mid t-1}$ and $Q_{t\mid t-1}$ are exactly the quantities the Kalman filter computes along the way, this **prediction-error decomposition** of the log-likelihood can be evaluated, for any trial $\theta$, by one forward pass of the filter, and then maximized numerically over $\theta$. ### A worked case: the local level model Take the local level model with $B_t=1,R_t=\sigma_\epsilon^2$ and write $\ell(\sigma_Z,\sigma_\epsilon):=-2\log L$. Two remarks make the filter's behaviour here more transparent. **Why large $\sigma_Z$ does not mean overfitting.** Since $Q_{t\mid t-1}=Q_{t-1\mid t-1}+\sigma_Z^2\ge\sigma_Z^2$, a large state-noise variance $\sigma_Z$ makes every $Q_{t\mid t-1}$ large, so the filter weight on $y_t$ in $m_{t\mid t}$ dominates the weight on $m_{t\mid t-1}$: $m_{t\mid t}\approx y_t$ for every $t$ when $\sigma_Z$ is large. One might worry that a model that simply reproduces the data is "overfitting" in the sense of having its likelihood improve without bound as $\sigma_Z\to\infty$. It does not: writing the likelihood in terms of $m_{t-1\mid t-1}\approx y_{t-1}$ for large $\sigma_Z$, $$\ell(\sigma_Z,\sigma_\epsilon) \approx \sum_{t=0}^T\left[\log\{2\pi(Q_{t-1\mid t-1}+\sigma_Z^2+\sigma_\epsilon^2)\}+\frac{(y_t-y_{t-1})^2}{Q_{t-1\mid t-1}+\sigma_Z^2+\sigma_\epsilon^2}\right],$$ and the log term grows with $\sigma_Z$ while the fraction shrinks, so the whole sum *increases* — the negative log-likelihood gets worse, not better, as $\sigma_Z\to\infty$. There is a genuine trade-off being optimized, not a free lunch at $\sigma_Z=\infty$. **A one-dimensional trick for a two-parameter search.** Optimizing $\ell(\sigma_Z,\sigma_\epsilon)$ directly over two parameters is more work than necessary. Under the diffuse initialization $C\to\infty$ (so the recursion starts from $m_{0\mid0}=y_0,Q_{0\mid0}=\sigma_\epsilon^2$ and only $t=1,\dots,T$ contribute to the objective, the $t=0$ term becoming an additive constant $\log(2\pi C)$ that drops out of the optimization), the following scaling identity holds: if $m_{t\mid t-1}(\sigma_Z,\sigma_\epsilon)$ and $Q_{t\mid t-1}(\sigma_Z,\sigma_\epsilon)$ denote the predictive mean and variance produced by this diffuse-start recursion, $$m_{t\mid t-1}(\sigma_Z,\sigma_\epsilon) = m_{t\mid t-1}\!\left(\frac{\sigma_Z}{\sigma_\epsilon},1\right), \qquad Q_{t\mid t-1}(\sigma_Z,\sigma_\epsilon) = \sigma_\epsilon^2\,Q_{t\mid t-1}\!\left(\frac{\sigma_Z}{\sigma_\epsilon},1\right) \tag{$\ast$}$$ (left as an exercise below). Writing $q:=\sigma_Z/\sigma_\epsilon$ and using $(\ast)$ to re-express the objective in terms of $q$ and $\sigma_\epsilon$ alone, minimizing over $\sigma_\epsilon^2$ for each fixed $q$ has the closed form $$\hat\sigma_\epsilon^2(q) = \frac1T\sum_{t=1}^T\frac{(y_t-m_{t\mid t-1}(q,1))^2}{Q_{t\mid t-1}(q,1)+1}.$$ Substituting this back leaves a genuinely one-dimensional objective to minimize numerically over $q>0$, $$T\log\big(2\pi\hat\sigma_\epsilon^2(q)\big)+\sum_{t=1}^T\log\big(Q_{t\mid t-1}(q,1)+1\big)+T.$$ Having found the minimizer $\hat q$, the parameter estimates are $\hat\sigma_\epsilon^2=\hat\sigma_\epsilon^2(\hat q)$ and $\hat\sigma_Z=\hat q\,\hat\sigma_\epsilon(\hat q)$. Each evaluation of this objective still requires running the Kalman filter once (with $\sigma_Z$ set to $q$ and $\sigma_\epsilon$ set to $1$), but the search itself is over a single variable rather than two. ## Recursive Bayesian regression without matrix inversion Consider ordinary Bayesian linear regression: data $(z_0,y_0),\dots,(z_T,y_T)$ with $z_t$ a $p\times1$ deterministic covariate, $y_t=z_t'\beta+\epsilon_t$, $\epsilon_t\stackrel{\text{i.i.d}}{\sim}N(0,\sigma_\epsilon^2)$, and prior $\beta\sim N(\mu_0,\Gamma_0)$ (with $\mu_0=0,\Gamma_0=CI$ for large $C$ if no prior information is available — useful in particular because the posterior stays well-defined even when the design matrix $Z$ is not full rank, unlike the least squares estimator). The posterior is $$\beta\mid\text{data} \sim N\!\left(\Big(\Gamma_0^{-1}+\tfrac{Z'Z}{\sigma_\epsilon^2}\Big)^{-1}\Big(\tfrac{Z'Y}{\sigma_\epsilon^2}+\Gamma_0^{-1}\mu_0\Big),\;\Big(\Gamma_0^{-1}+\tfrac{Z'Z}{\sigma_\epsilon^2}\Big)^{-1}\right),$$ which requires inverting a $p\times p$ matrix directly. Writing this as a state space model gives an alternative that never inverts anything larger than a scalar. Take the state to be static, $\beta_t=\beta_{t-1}$ for $t=1,2,\dots$ (so $A_t=I$, $\Sigma_t=0$), with observation $y_t=z_t'\beta_t+\epsilon_t$ and initial condition $\beta_0\sim N(\mu_0,\Gamma_0)$; this is exactly the Bayesian regression model above, and the filtering distribution at time $T$ is the posterior. Because the state does not move, the time update is trivial, $m_{t\mid t-1}=m_{t-1\mid t-1}$, $Q_{t\mid t-1}=Q_{t-1\mid t-1}$, and the measurement update (using the Woodbury form, since $y_t$ is scalar) is $$m_{t\mid t} = m_{t\mid t-1}+\frac{y_t-z_t'm_{t\mid t-1}}{z_t'Q_{t\mid t-1}z_t+\sigma_\epsilon^2}\,Q_{t\mid t-1}z_t, \qquad Q_{t\mid t} = Q_{t\mid t-1}-\frac{Q_{t\mid t-1}z_tz_t'Q_{t\mid t-1}}{z_t'Q_{t\mid t-1}z_t+\sigma_\epsilon^2},$$ initialized from $m_{0\mid-1}=\mu_0,\,Q_{0\mid-1}=\Gamma_0$. At every step the only division is by the scalar $z_t'Q_{t\mid t-1}z_t+\sigma_\epsilon^2$: the Kalman filter reaches the same posterior as the direct formula while never inverting a $p\times p$ matrix — only matrix-vector products and one scalar inversion per observation. ## Prediction, and a look ahead to smoothing For $s>t$, the prediction distribution $X_s\mid Y_{0:t}=y_{0:t}$ is obtained by repeating the time update forward from $m_{t\mid t},Q_{t\mid t}$ without any further measurement updates: for $s=t+1,t+2,\dots$, $$m_{s\mid t} = A_sm_{s-1\mid t}, \qquad Q_{s\mid t} = A_sQ_{s-1\mid t}A_s'+\Sigma_s,$$ using $m_{t\mid t},Q_{t\mid t}$ to start the recursion. This is nothing more than the time update applied repeatedly with no intervening data. Smoothing distributions ($s\le t$) are the remaining piece of the FFBS strategy outlined earlier: the last one, $X_T\mid Y_{0:T}=y_{0:T}$, is already produced by the forward filtering pass, and the rest are obtained by a **backward** recursion from $s=T-1$ down to $s=0$. That backward recursion — its general form, and its closed-form specialization for linear Gaussian models — is genuinely the next topic and is not covered by the material collected in this chapter. ## Exercises 1. In the acceleration-model tracking example, the local linear model was recovered by dropping a negligible term and rewriting the resulting second-difference recursion as a state space model in two different ways: with state $(x_{k,1},x_{k-1,1})$, and with state $(x_{k,1},\,(\Delta t)^{-1}(x_{k,1}-x_{k-1,1}))$. Write out the Kalman filter recursions (time update, measurement update, and initialization) for the local linear model in each of these two parametrizations, and check that they produce the same filtered estimate of the position $x_{k,1}$. 2. Prove the scaling identity $(\ast)$ used to reduce the local level model's likelihood optimization to a search over one parameter: with the diffuse initialization $m_{0\mid0}=y_0,\,Q_{0\mid0}=\sigma_\epsilon^2$, show that the Kalman filter's one-step predictive mean and variance satisfy $m_{t\mid t-1}(\sigma_Z,\sigma_\epsilon)=m_{t\mid t-1}(\sigma_Z/\sigma_\epsilon,1)$ and $Q_{t\mid t-1}(\sigma_Z,\sigma_\epsilon)=\sigma_\epsilon^2\,Q_{t\mid t-1}(\sigma_Z/\sigma_\epsilon,1)$. ## Sources All material is from Aditya Guntuboyina's *Full Lecture Notes*, Spring 2022 UC Berkeley time series course (STAT 248), lectures one through eight, as reconstructed in this library's `FullNotes248Spring2022TimeSeries` conversion.
